docs.title: Out-of-Process Introspection Engine Architecture Specification
docs.text: This document establishes the technical design requirements, memory mapping matrices, and validation logs for building a host-side memory extraction platform targeting hardware-assisted virtualization layers.

docs.title: Strategic Goals
docs.text:
• Zero Guest-Side Footprint: Maintain absolute isolation by operating entirely from the Windows Host layer. The target operating system must remain completely unmodified.
  • Immune to Guest Attestation: Avoid using user-mode function hooks, guest-side debugging pipelines (Frida/GDB), or modifying guest-mode storage files. This ensures total immunity against internal guest application integrity checks and hardware attestation frameworks.
  • Hardware-Assisted Introspection: Bypass software-layer scanning by leveraging native processor execution tables and operating system object descriptors to locate live targets.

docs.title: Architectural Summary
docs.text:
Virtualization systems enforce hardware-level isolation barriers to convince the guest operating system it owns physical processing silicon. Rather than attempting to break this barrier from the inside, this SDK treats the entire running virtual machine as a raw, sequential pool of host-allocated bytes.

By emulating a hardware Memory Management Unit (MMU) directly inside our host application, we can read, translate, and verify live execution threads completely out-of-process.

docs.title: 👁️ The Host-Side Perspective Hierarchy
docs.text:
When performing Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI), every single execution layer exists exclusively as raw, flat bytes sitting inside standard PC physical RAM sticks. True physical hardware isolation does not exist inside user-mode software; instead, virtualization systems are nested execution boundaries designed to convince the guest environment it owns real silicon hardware.

From the host perspective looking downward, the simulation tiers stack sequentially:

  [ THE HOST PERSPECTIVE: WINDOWS 10/11 & YOUR AVALONIA APP ]
   │
   ▼ ──► Reads raw bytes out of MuMuNxDevice.exe using Win32 API handles.
  [ THE HYPERVISOR BOUNDARY: INTEL EPT / AMD SLAT TABLES ]
   │
   ▼ ──► Translates instruction sets and cuts Windows pages into virtual RAM pools.
  [ THE GUEST OS SPHERE: ANDROID 15 KERNEL LINUX RUNTIME ]
   │
   ▼ ──► Manages process descriptors and splits its virtual hardware layout via TTBR0_EL1.
  [ THE APPLICATION SPHERE: NATIVE GAME RUNTIME IL2CPP V31 ]
        ──► Calculates scrambled ARM pointers, processes HybridCLR tables, expands Brotli data.

docs.title: 🧱 The Functional Division Matrix
docs.text:
To prevent the architectural drift that causes monolithic programs to fail, responsibilities are strictly split by their execution domain. If a live data stream returns garbage, this boundary layout allows you to verify your hypervisor vision independently of the game's obfuscation layer.

Shared Introspection Engineering Domains

Structural Layer What it Sees / Manages What it Believes System Responsibility Game Plugin Space Obfuscated ARM64 pointers, Brotli data blocks, HybridCLR tables. "I am executing pure ARM64 code on a native, secure mobile device phone configuration." Reverse-Engineering Sandbox: Unscrambles game-specific loops and extracts typed data metrics. Core SDK Space Win32 Process handles, page allocations, Linux kernel task arrays, ARM64 page tables. "I am managing physical hardware registers, MMIO mapping paths, and system scheduler loops." Virtual Hardware Emulator: Translates Guest Virtual Addresses all the way down to Host Virtual Addresses.

docs.title: 🧭 Invariant Validation Protocol
docs.text:
Isolating Core SDK Faults from Game Obfuscation Faults

The Core SDK provides an isolated verification loop that completely ignores the target game binary. It scans high kernel memory for the static signature swapper\0 and checks PID == 0.

  • If the Core SDK can read the invariant Linux kernel string: Your Win32 process mapping, hypervisor translation layer, and ARM64 page table walker are 100% correct. Do not touch your core infrastructure. Any data errors reside entirely inside your plugin's game decryption loops.
  • If the Core SDK cannot read the kernel string: Your infrastructure lens is unaligned or blind. Do not touch your game plugin code; focus entirely on adjusting your core unmanaged layout sweeps against your third-party VMMap utility records.

docs.title: 🛠️ SDK Overview: Structural Architecture
docs.text:
The instrumentation engine is split across three distinct operational layers wrapped in a modular C# / Rust software development kit:

Core Engine Pipeline Mapping

graph TD
    subgraph Host_SDK [External Core SDK Module Workspace]
        M1["TargetMonitor Module<br>CLI Orchestration"] --> M2["MemoryMapper Module<br>Boundary Isolation"]
        M2 --> M3["MmuEmulator Module<br>Page Table Walker"]
    end

    subgraph Windows_Kernel [Layer A: Host Operating System]
        M2 --> L1["Query: VirtualQueryEx"] --> HVA["Isolate Host Virtual Address Blocks"]
    end

    subgraph Hypervisor [Layer B: Silicon Hardware]
        M3 --> L2["Query: Manual PTW Walk"] --> GPA["Resolve Guest Physical Address"]
    end
  1. TargetMonitor: Automates system token parsing and coordinates instance diagnostics to scrape active configurations.
  2. MemoryMapper: Performs un-opinionated allocation sweeps to dynamically isolate hypervisor hardware memory segments.
  3. MmuEmulator: Re-creates multi-level paging tables out-of-process to translate virtual runtime metrics into invariant host coordinates.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering Workflow & Multi-Tool Provenance
docs.text: This document establishes the strict multi-tool reverse engineering pipeline used to verify memory structures, cryptographic keys, and pointer offsets prior to code initialization.

docs.title: 🧭 The Core Mandate: Proved Reality Before Code
docs.text:
Operational Workflow Imperative

No project files, classes, or code block implementations may be written inside the C# solution workspace based on raw assumptions or unverified guesses.

Every structural offset, bit-shift mask, or decryption algorithm must pass through our multi-tool verification pipeline first. Once proven, the findings are permanently recorded in this documentation suite, which then serves as the absolute blueprint for our production code.

docs.title: 🛠️ The Multi-Tool Verification Workbench
docs.text:
Our reverse engineering pipeline leverages distinct software execution suites to cross-verify memory data completely independent of the main C# runtime environment:

  [ Target App Binary & Assets ] ──► [ Ghidra Static Disassembly ] ──► Uncovers Structural Layouts & Keys
                                                                               │
                                                                               ▼ (Map to Live State)
  [ Live Hypervisor Memory    ] ──► [ Cheat Engine & Lua Scripts ] ──► Validates Pointers and Memory Sweeps
                                                                               │
                                                                               ▼ (Prototype Cryptography)
  [ Extracted Stream Buffers  ] ──► [ Python Script Prototyping ]  ──► Proves Brotli / De-obfuscation Math
                                                                               │
                                                                               ▼ (Lock Into Blueprint)
  [ Invariant Specifications  ] ──► [ MkDocs Material Documentation]──► Production C# Code Mirror

docs.title: 1. Static Binaries & Structural Reversing (Ghidra Layer)
docs.text:
• Tactical Focus: Extracting libil2cpp.so and processing it alongside dumped metadata headers to discover static types.
  • Operational Output: Identifies how the game binary obfuscates its data layouts, maps the HybridCLR interpreter execution tables, and uncovers cryptographic initialization keys used for raw file decryption.

docs.title: 2. Live Memory State Validation (Cheat Engine & Lua Pipeline)
docs.text:
• Tactical Focus: Attaching directly to the host hypervisor process workspace (MuMuNxDevice.exe) to execute real-time address validation.
  • Operational Output: Utilizing the internal Cheat Engine Lua engine to script manual 4-level page table walks and test pointer-crawling paths directly within CE. This proves our hardware mapping math matches live execution byte-for-byte before we ever write a C# memory driver loop.

docs.title: 3. Crypotographic & Compression Prototyping (Python Stream Layer)
docs.text:
• Tactical Focus: Executing rapid data-manipulation passes over raw memory streams dumped by our reversing tools.
  • Operational Output: Python scripts test the parsing loops, handle bit-shifting equations, and execute Brotli stream decompression against actual raw game data packets. This eliminates marshalling or compiler quirks from masking our initial logic flaws.

docs.title: ⚠️ Architectural Invariants for AI Collaboration
docs.text:
AI Directives for the Prototyping Phase

  • The Documentation Invariant: When tasked with analyzing an obfuscated structure or writing a parsing algorithm, the AI must base its logic entirely on verified inputs extracted from your Ghidra, Python, or Cheat Engine logs.
  • Anti-Guessing Gatekeeper: If a layout is unverified, the AI must help you construct a specific Cheat Engine Lua snippet or a Python diagnostic script to test the assumption against live bytes first, keeping your C# project workspace completely pristine and free of experimental clutter.

docs.title: Ch.1.4 - Layer D: Application Runtime
docs.text:
VMI Architectural Anchor

Game Plugin Responsibility: This layer is the execution space of your dedicated, separate dynamic link library (DLL) plugins. Because the Core SDK provides a clear window past Layers A, B, and C, your plugin can analyze Layer D variables as flat memory, focusing entirely on reversing IL2CPP v31 tables, HybridCLR interpreters, and Brotli structures.

docs.title: 1.1 The Target Execution Environment
docs.text: Layer D represents the target execution space where user-mode applications run. The application processes operate using standard 64-bit ARM virtual memory pointers (e.g., 0x0000007F1A2B3C4D).

docs.title: 1.2 Dynamic Shifting Constraints
docs.text:
The application layer frequently executes obfuscation patterns, virtualized execution loops, and runtime memory shifts to hinder traditional software reverse engineering tools.

Bypassing Guest Protections via Layer A

Because this application layer remains strictly bounded by the guest operating system's hardware page tables, it is physically impossible for the application to hide its memory cells from an external host tool operating down in Layer A.

The game code can apply complex loops to scramble its pointers inside its own virtual space, but down at the hardware translation layer, a value must resolve to a physical memory cell for the processor to execute it. Our SDK monitors that cell directly from the outside, rendering guest-side detection routines completely useless.

docs.title: Ch.1.1 - Layer A: Host Virtual Workspace
docs.text:
VMI Architectural Anchor

Core SDK Responsibility: This host layer is mapped exclusively by the MemoryMapper service. The isolated 1.5625 GB and 3.4375 GB segments discovered here are cached immediately to anchor all downstream ARM64 page-table walking routines.

docs.title: Ch.1.1 - Layer A: Host Virtual Workspace
1.1 The Execution Root
docs.text: Layer A represents the absolute execution root of our introspection engine. The entire target virtual phone environment is spawned, sustained, and maintained by a standard Windows user-mode worker process named MuMuNxDevice.exe.

docs.title: 1.2 Unmanaged Memory Allocations
docs.text:
To feed raw physical RAM data bytes down to the processor's hardware execution pipelines, this worker process commits massive, unmanaged memory blocks within its private host process workspace.

The Host Memory Mapping Reality

While the guest operating system believes it is reading raw electrical storage cells, those bytes actually reside inside standard memory pages allocated directly to your PC's physical RAM sticks. If the SDK can programmatically identify the exact Host Virtual Address (HVA) base where this container sits, we obtain a direct, invisible window straight into the live target memory space.

docs.title: 1.3 Target Boundary Isolation Rules
docs.text:
To ensure the SDK relies on zero hardcoded sizes or temporary offsets that break across individual software version updates, the mapping module evaluates the host workspace dynamically using two strict execution parameters:

  • Boundary State Analysis: The SDK runs a linear sweep across the active process allocations. It instantly filters out normal application binaries (MEM_IMAGE) and active web-overlay rendering heaps by isolating blocks where State == MEM_COMMIT and Protect == PAGE_READWRITE.
  • Allocation Type Profiling: The guest hardware blocks are generated as anonymous virtual memory sections. The engine profiles the mapping descriptor signatures, targeting regions flagged specifically as MEM_PRIVATE (Private Data) or anonymous pagefile backing layers.

docs.title: Ch.1.2 - Layer B: Hypervisor EPT Map
docs.text:
VMI Architectural Anchor

Core SDK Responsibility: The \(GPA \longrightarrow HVA\) conditional translation logic defined here is handled explicitly by the HypervisorRouter service. It bridges the hardware MMIO hole before guest kernel structures are parsed.

docs.title: Ch.1.2 - Layer B: Hypervisor EPT Map
1.1 Second Level Address Translation (SLAT / EPT)
docs.text:
Layer B is the hardware translation bridge enforced at the silicon layer of the CPU socket. Modern processors run hardware virtual machines using Second Level Address Translation (SLAT), which Intel designates as EPT (Extended Page Tables).

The CPU splits memory translation into two entirely independent hierarchies managed concurrently inside the silicon chip:

Hardware CPU Paging Separation

  • CR3 / TTBR0_EL1: Handles Guest Virtual Address to Guest Physical Address conversions (\(GVA \longrightarrow GPA\)) managed inside the guest operating system.
  • EPT Pointer: Handles Guest Physical Address to Host Physical Address conversions (\(GPA \longrightarrow HPA\)) managed by the Windows Kernel.

docs.title: 1.2 Layer B ──> Layer A Routing Mathematical Logic
docs.text:
The relationship between what the Guest OS sees as a Physical Address and how it maps to your Windows Host addresses follows a predictable structure due to the virtual MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O) Gap. This gap splits the Guest Physical Address (GPA) space into two segments to prevent guest operating system memory boundaries from overlapping with underlying virtualized hardware registers.

Memory Architecture Block Mapping

graph TD
    subgraph GPA [Layer B: Guest Physical Address Space]
        A[0x00000000<br>Lower System Space<br>Size: 1.5625 GB] --> L1["Offset: 0x64000000"] --> B[Virtual Hardware / MMIO Hole<br>Trapped by Hypervisor]
        B --> L2["Offset: 0x80000000"] --> C[Upper Main App Space<br>Size: 3.4375 GB]
    end

    subgraph HVA [Layer A: Windows Host RAM Blocks]
        D[(1.5625 GB Host Buffer Pointer)]
        E[(3.4375 GB Host Buffer Pointer)]
    end

    A -->|"[Rule A: Direct Map]"| D
    C -->|"[Rule B: GPA - 0x80000000]"| E

Because of this architectural gap, the SDK applies an internal conditional branch logic model to route GPA lookups to the correct Windows memory buffer:

Layer B ──> Layer A Translation Algorithm

public static class HypervisorRouter
{
    // Core Hardware Boundary Memory Offsets
    private const ulong MmioHoleStart = 0x64000000;
    private const ulong UpperRamStart = 0x80000000;

    /// <summary>
    /// Translates a Guest Physical Address (GPA) to a readable Host Virtual Address (HVA).
    /// </summary>
    public static IntPtr TranslateGpaToHva(ulong gpa, IntPtr lowerBaseHva, IntPtr upperBaseHva)
    {
        // CASE 1: Lower System Memory Range Translation
        if (gpa < MmioHoleStart)
        {
            return new IntPtr(lowerBaseHva.ToInt64() + (long)gpa);
        }

        // CASE 2: Upper Application Space Translation (Active Engine Pool)
        if (gpa >= UpperRamStart)
        {
            ulong memoryOffset = gpa - UpperRamStart;
            return new IntPtr(upperBaseHva.ToInt64() + (long)memoryOffset);
        }

        // CASE 3: Hardware Exception Catch Boundary
        throw new InvalidOperationException(
            \$"Access violation: GPA 0x{gpa:X} trapped inside MMIO hardware gap."
        );
    }
}

docs.title: Ch.1.3 - Layer C: Android Physical RAM
docs.text:
VMI Architectural Anchor

Core SDK Responsibility: This kernel tier is the tracking domain of the TaskEnumerator service. It sweeps this space out-of-process for system signatures to isolate the target game's Page Global Directory (PGD) root pointer.

docs.title: Ch.1.3 - Layer C: Guest Android Kernel Physical Space
1.1 The Virtual-to-Physical Kernel Map
docs.text:
Layer C marks the boundary of the simulated operating system. The Android Linux kernel treats the hardware partition block it receives from the hypervisor as its entire pool of physical RAM.

Inside this space, the kernel manages a virtual memory configuration to isolate low-level system tracking files from user-mode applications:

Guest Operating System Virtual Segmentation

graph LR
    subgraph GVA [Layer C: Guest Virtual Address Space Range]
        A["0x0000000000000000<br>User Space Area<br>Applications & Native Games"] --> L1["Hardware Virtual Gap Boundary"]
        L1 --> B["0x0000008000000000<br>Unmapped Space<br>Unallocated Memory Pool"]
        B --> L2["High Kernel Space Map"]
        L2 --> C["0xFFFF000000000000<br>Kernel Space Area<br>Drivers & Linked Task Lists"]
    end

docs.title: 1.2 Contiguous Aggregate Consolidation
docs.text: Because an operating system requires a flat physical layout to initialize its hardware kernel, the guest RAM splits will consistently present as the single largest, contiguous allocations in the entire target process workspace. By grouping these massive, adjacent segments dynamically at launch, your SDK calculates any user memory modifications (whether the emulator is configured to 3GB, 5GB, or 8GB of RAM) completely automatically.

docs.title: 1.1 Out-of-Process Introspection Strategy
docs.text: When performing un-opinionated memory diagnostics from the host side, the SDK targets the guest operating system's internal process scheduling arrays. Because user-space address maps shift dynamically at runtime, the application must identify target environments programmatically using the kernel's native task layouts.

docs.title: 1.2 The 64-Bit Process Descriptor Layout
docs.text:
Every execution thread, worker task, and application running inside the Linux guest environment is represented by a central process descriptor block. For a standard 64-bit ARM Linux kernel configuration, the fields tracked during a memory audit are aligned to predictable byte offsets relative to the structure's base address:

Field Name Type / Structure Byte Offset Architectural Purpose task_state volatile long 0x00 Tracks active scheduler execution state flags task_list struct list_head 0x30 Circular doubly-linked list nodes (next/prev pointers) mm_map struct mm_struct* 0x480 Pointer to the process's active user-mode memory descriptor process_id int 0x4C8 The unique Linux Process ID (PID) tracking token process_comm char[16] 0x6A0 Alphanumeric string tag tracking the executable package name

docs.title: 1.3 C# Structural Representation
docs.text:
To read these variables out-of-process without violating type safety, the SDK core mirrors this geometry using explicit sequential structure fields:

using System;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

namespace MuMuSDK.Core.Models
{
    [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential, Pack = 1)]
    public struct TaskDescriptor
    {
        // Padded layout tracking offsets up to list handles
        [MarshalAs(UnmanagedType.ByValArray, SizeConst = 0x30)]
        private byte[] _pad0;

        // Linked list handle: Offset 0x30
        public IntPtr NextTask;
        public IntPtr PrevTask;

        // Padded layout tracking list descriptors to memory mapping handles
        [MarshalAs(UnmanagedType.ByValArray, SizeConst = 0x438)]
        private byte[] _pad1;

        // Pointer to active memory descriptor: Offset 0x480
        public IntPtr MemoryMapPointer;

        // Process Identifier field: Offset 0x4C8
        public int ProcessId;

        // Padded layout tracking process ID to the communication label string
        [MarshalAs(UnmanagedType.ByValArray, SizeConst = 0x1D4)]
        private byte[] _pad2;

        // Alphanumeric process executable tag: Offset 0x6A0
        [MarshalAs(UnmanagedType.ByValArray, SizeConst = 16)]
        public byte[] ProcessCommName;
    }
}

docs.title: 1.1 Locating the Memory Manager Descriptor
docs.text: Once the task loop isolates the specific process node for the target application, it reads the 64-bit reference address stored at offset 0x480 (MemoryMapPointer). If this value is completely null (0x0), it indicates a pure background kernel worker thread; user-mode environments will always return a valid memory manager pointer.

docs.title: 1.2 Resolving the Page Global Directory (PGD)
docs.text:
Following this pointer down into the memory block allows the engine to parse the application's underlying memory descriptors. Inside this sub-structure lies the key register mapping point:

Field Reference Data Type Structural Offset Architectural / Hardware Function users_count atomic_t 0x00 Tracks active shared threads referencing this map pgd_base entry_t* 0x40 Root pointer to the 4-level page table structure

The 64-bit value located at offset 0x40 represents the Page Global Directory (PGD) root. On a physical phone, this exact coordinate maps to the hardware register index loaded into the CPU's TTBR0_EL1 configuration space whenever that application is active.

Hardware Root Mapping Matrix

graph LR
    subgraph Layer_C [Layer C: Process Descriptor]
        A["task_struct Node<br>Offset 0x480"] --> B["mm_struct Map Pointer<br>Offset 0x40"]
    end
    subgraph Layer_B [Layer B: Hypervisor EPT Base]
        B --> C["pgd_base Root Address<br>Guest Physical Address"]
    end
    subgraph Target [Translation Input]
        C --> D["Chapter 3 Paging Engine<br>Translation Table Target"]
    end

docs.title: 1.3 C# PGD Extraction Blueprint
docs.text:
Your SDK reads this value out-of-process to fetch the permanent anchor point needed to drive your bit-shifting address translation calculations:

C# PGD Anchor Resolution Routines

public static class PgdResolver
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Extracts the raw Page Global Directory Guest Physical Address from an isolated task node.
    /// </summary>
    public static ulong ExtractPgdBaseAddress(IntPtr targetTaskNode, IntPtr upperBaseHva)
    {
        // 1. Fetch the mm_struct pointer from task_struct offset 0x480
        IntPtr mmStructGpa = ReadPointer(targetTaskNode + 0x480);
        if (mmStructGpa == IntPtr.Zero) return 0;

        // 2. Convert memory map GPA pointer handle to standard Host Virtual Address space
        IntPtr mmStructHva = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva((ulong)mmStructGpa, IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);

        // 3. Extract the master pgd_base address from mm_struct offset 0x40
        ulong rawPgdBaseGpa = ReadUInt64(mmStructHva + 0x40);

        // This resolved ulong is your invariant translation table root anchor!
        return rawPgdBaseGpa;
    }
}

docs.title: 1.1 Walking the Task Array List
docs.text: The task_list field handles scheduling execution metrics via a standard circular doubly-linked list (struct list_head). Because the entries form an unbroken loop, the engine must look for a static system anchor to start searching without encountering infinite loop index limits.

docs.title: 1.2 Finding the Kernel Signature (The "Swapper" Task Search)
docs.text:
Process ID 0 (known as the swapper task or init_task) is statically compiled directly into the kernel binary space. To isolate it dynamically entirely from the Windows host layer, the scanner sweeps high-memory blocks (0xFFFF...) for a unique identifier string signature:

Kernel Signature Scanner Pipeline

graph TD
    A["Scan High-Memory Regions"] --> B["Verify Offset 0x6A0<br>Matches 'swapper\0'?"]
    B --> C["Verify Offset 0x4C8<br>Matches ProcessId == 0?"]
    C --> D["Isolate Anchor Node Pointer<br>Return Target GVA Anchor"]

docs.title: 1.3 The C# Task Enumeration Engine Logic
docs.text:
Once your C# framework locks onto this structural anchor node, it uses a non-intrusive loop to traverse the active process chains and identify target runtimes.

C# Out-of-Process Task Chain Enumeration

using System;
using MuMuSDK.Core.Services; // (1)

namespace MuMuSDK.Core.Services
{
    public static class TaskChainEnumerator
    {
        /// <summary>
        /// Traverses the guest kernel doubly-linked task list to extract a target process node pointer.
        /// </summary>
        public static IntPtr FindTargetProcessNode(IntPtr anchorNode, string targetName, IntPtr upperBaseHva)
        {
            IntPtr currentNode = anchorNode;

            do
            {
                // 1. Read process name character string buffer metrics
                string currentCommName = ReadProcessCommName(currentNode);

                if (currentCommName.Equals(targetName, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
                {
                    // Success: Target identifier discovered cleanly
                    return currentNode;
                }

                // 2. Extract next circular task entry pointer handle from offset 0x30
                IntPtr guestPhysicalNext = ReadPointer(currentNode + 0x30);

                // 3. Convert extracted GPA handle to high-level Host Virtual Address via our native core service helper
                currentNode = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva((ulong)guestPhysicalNext, IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);

            } while (currentNode != anchorNode);

            return IntPtr.Zero; // Context not discovered inside the current scheduling cycle
        }

        // Primitive placeholders matching your low-level verification drivers
        private static string ReadProcessCommName(IntPtr nodeHva) => throw new NotImplementedException();
        private static IntPtr ReadPointer(IntPtr addressHva) => throw new NotImplementedException();
    }
}
  1. 🔍 Structural resolution helpers like HypervisorRouter reside safely in the internal invariant MuMuSDK.Core.Services namespace wrapper.

docs.title: 1.1 Emulating the Hardware MMU Loop
docs.text:
To resolve an ARM64 application pointer completely out-of-process from the host, the SDK must traverse the 4-level table hierarchy sequentially inside the raw byte stream pool.

graph TD
    A["Extract PGD Base Root"] -->|Apply Bits 47:39| B["Read PUD Base Address"]
    B -->|Apply Bits 38:30| C["Read PMD Base Address"]
    C -->|Apply Bits 29:21| D["Read PTE Base Address"]
    D -->|Apply Bits 20:12| E["Extract Output Frame Number"]
    E -->|Append Offset 11:0| F["Resolved Guest Physical Address (GPA)"]

docs.title: 1.2 Descriptor Scaling Calculations
docs.text:
Because every entry within an execution table consumes exactly 8 bytes in a 64-bit architecture, the relative offset point is shifted left by 3 bits (<< 3):

\[\text{Entry Memory Address} = \text{Table Base Address} + (\text{Index} \times 8)\]

docs.title: 1.3 C# Page Table Walking Engine Blueprint
docs.text:
The framework emulates this multi-tiered look-up engine using explicit conditional block transitions:

C# Out-of-Process 4-Level Page Table Walker

public static class HardwareMmuEmulator
{
    public static ulong TranslateVirtualToPhysical(ulong gva, ulong pgdBaseGpa, IntPtr upperBaseHva)
    {
        // 1. Break down incoming GVA target into component layout indices
        var coordinates = AddressDisassembler.SplitVirtualAddress(gva);

        // 2. Traversal Loop Tier 1: PGD -> PUD
        IntPtr pgdEntryHva = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva(pgdBaseGpa + (coordinates.PgdIndex * 8), IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);
        ulong pudBaseGpa = MemoryReader.ReadUInt64(pgdEntryHva) & 0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL; // Extract output physical framing address masks

        // 3. Traversal Loop Tier 2: PUD -> PMD
        IntPtr pudEntryHva = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva(pudBaseGpa + (coordinates.PudIndex * 8), IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);
        ulong pmdBaseGpa = MemoryReader.ReadUInt64(pudEntryHva) & 0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL;

        // 4. Traversal Loop Tier 3: PMD -> PTE
        IntPtr pmdEntryHva = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva(pmdBaseGpa + (coordinates.PmdIndex * 8), IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);
        ulong pteBaseGpa = MemoryReader.ReadUInt64(pmdEntryHva) & 0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL;

        // 5. Traversal Loop Tier 4: PTE -> Physical Page Frame Base
        IntPtr pteEntryHva = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva(pteBaseGpa + (coordinates.PteIndex * 8), IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva);
        ulong physicalFrameBaseGpa = MemoryReader.ReadUInt64(pteEntryHva) & 0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL;

        // 6. Append lower page relative offset to isolate absolute GPA coordinate
        return physicalFrameBaseGpa + coordinates.PageOffset;
    }
}

docs.title: 1.1 Address Deconstruction
docs.text: Under a standard 48-bit virtual address layout on an ARM64 Android kernel, a virtual address pointer functions as a collection of coordinates rather than a flat number. The processor cuts a 64-bit pointer into 9-bit indexing spans to navigate its translation hierarchies.

docs.title: 1.2 Bit Span Allocation Schema
docs.text:
Using native Material markdown features, the complete layout parsing matrix tracks coordinates across explicit bit positions:

Segment Block Name Targeted Bit Range Coordinate Bit Width Purpose / Table Destination Sign Extension [63:48] 16 Bits Distinguishes User-space (0x0000) vs Kernel-space (0xFFFF) maps PGD Index [47:39] 9 Bits Offset coordinate within the root Page Global Directory PUD Index [38:30] 9 Bits Offset coordinate within the Page Upper Directory PMD Index [29:21] 9 Bits Offset coordinate within the Page Middle Directory PTE Index [20:12] 9 Bits Offset coordinate within the final hardware Page Table Entry Page Offset [11:0] 12 Bits Direct relative byte address offset inside the 4096-byte target RAM cell

docs.title: 1.3 C# Disassembly Logic Routines
docs.text:
Your core SDK disassembles these segments cleanly using high-performance bitwise right shifts combined with an extraction mask matching 0x1FF:

public static class AddressDisassembler
{
    private const ulong IndexMask = 0x1FF;   // Selects exactly 9 bits of precision (512 total slices)
    private const ulong OffsetMask = 0xFFF;  // Selects exactly 12 bits of lower page offset tracking

    public static DecoupledCoordinates SplitVirtualAddress(ulong gva)
    {
        return new DecoupledCoordinates
        {
            PgdIndex   = (gva >> 39) & IndexMask,
            PudIndex   = (gva >> 30) & IndexMask,
            PmdIndex   = (gva >> 21) & IndexMask,
            PteIndex   = (gva >> 12) & IndexMask,
            PageOffset = gva & OffsetMask
        };
    }
}

public struct DecoupledCoordinates
{
    public ulong PgdIndex;
    public ulong PudIndex;
    public ulong PmdIndex;
    public ulong PteIndex;
    public ulong PageOffset;
}

docs.title: 1.1 The Out-of-Process Task Discovery Hurdle
docs.text: Because the Linux kernel shifts its structural storage boundaries slightly upon every clean boot sequence, the engine implements a signature routine to isolate the root execution context dynamically.

docs.title: 1.2 Targeting the Process Chain Anchor
docs.text:
The root of all scheduling records inside a Linux system maps to process ID 0, the swapper task/init_task. This specific descriptor is statically compiled directly inside the high-memory kernel data sections.

Isolating the Anchor Node completely from Windows

The SDK sweeps the high-memory boundary space (0xFFFF...) looking for the unique 8-byte ASCII character tracking array: s w a p p e r \0. Once located, it verifies that the signed integer tracking the process ID reads exactly 0, locking onto the head node of the system process chain.

docs.title: 1.3 C# Process Search Engine Iterations
docs.text:
Once the init_task block anchor is locked, your C# SDK code loops through the doubly-linked process array lists out-of-process to find your target target package framework:

public static class TargetProcessLocator
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Audits the active kernel process matrix lists to locate specific execution package references.
    /// </summary>
    public static IntPtr FindActiveAppNode(IntPtr initTaskHva, string packageCommName, IntPtr upperBaseHva)
    {
        IntPtr currentTask = initTaskHva;

        while (currentTask != IntPtr.Zero)
        {
            // 1. Extract Process Comm Tag Name string from current task node
            string commName = ReadCommString(currentTask + 0x6A0);

            if (commName.Equals(packageCommName, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            {
                // Target discovered! Return the active task descriptor block address.
                return currentTask;
            }

            // 2. Fetch adjacent task node link from the linked-list tracker at offset 0x30
            ulong nextTaskGpa = MemoryReader.ReadUInt64(currentTask + 0x30);

            // 3. Resolve extracted pointer back to target Host Virtual Address mapping coordinates
            currentTask = HypervisorRouter.TranslateGpaToHva(nextTaskGpa, IntPtr.Zero, upperBaseHva) - 0x30;
        }

        return IntPtr.Zero;
    }
}

By implementing our memory diagnostics framework at this level, we decouple our utility entirely from the application layer execution loops.

  • Complete Isolation: Because our reading mechanism interacts exclusively with unmanaged memory pages owned by the host hypervisor process, it remains completely invisible to guest security frameworks. The target environment cannot intercept or scan your utility because the code runs entirely outside its virtualization context.

docs.title: AI Engineering Guardrails & Prompt Instructions
docs.text: This page serves as an invariant context anchor for artificial intelligence collaborators. When generating, refactoring, or evaluating code blocks for this repository, the AI must strictly adhere to these operational boundaries.

docs.title: 🚫 Absolute Refusal Thresholds
docs.text:
Forbidden AI Actions

  • Do Not Collapse Layers: Never merge, nest, or embed game-specific decryption algorithms or IL2CPP signature configurations inside the MuMuSDK.Core or MuMuSDK.CLI namespaces.
  • Do Not Inject Win32 into Plugins: If requested to optimize or write a pointer-solving engine inside a game-specific plugin library, the AI must refuse to introduce P/Invoke signatures (OpenProcess, ReadProcessMemory, VirtualQueryEx) into that assembly space.
  • Do Not Autocomplete Hardware Masks: Do not invent, guess, or modify the physical page-walking masks (0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL) or memory boundary constants (0x64000000) without explicit confirmation that the underlying Android 15 kernel layout has shifted.

docs.title: 🏗️ Companion Tooling and Standalone Solution Boundaries
docs.text:
To maintain maximum execution stability, the tools tracking static disk assets must remain completely separate from the real-time Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI) pipeline.

Static vs. Dynamic Workspace Separation

  • The Standalone File Decryptor: Any utility built to unpack, decrypt, or parse local file assets (global-metadata.dat / libil2cpp.so) must be maintained in a completely separate Visual Studio solution workspace.
  • The Communication Pipeline: The standalone file tool executes entirely offline. It extracts obfuscated string pools or header magic byte layers, and outputs a flat, readable data payload (e.g., a serialized offsets.json configuration block).
  • The Runtime Plugin Consumption: The target game plugin in the main solution references only this serialized output file. It reads the clean offsets at startup, completely freeing your live memory scanning loop from carrying heavy static file parsing or desktop disassembly dependencies.

  • Defensive Service Mapping: When writing service registrations for the cross-project inversion container, always ensure services are mapped under their respective abstract interface boundaries to prevent concrete class coupling.

docs.title: Hypervisor Isolation & Hardware Validation Checkpoints
docs.text: This document establishes the strict diagnostic validation rules required to verify the host-side hypervisor abstraction layer independently of game-specific metadata decryption or HybridCLR obfuscation hooks.

docs.title: 🧭 The Single Point of Truth Mandate
docs.text:
To isolate hypervisor mapping failures from game obfuscation failures, the Core SDK must provide explicit, native validation routines that prove the \(GVA \longrightarrow GPA \longrightarrow HVA\) mapping pipeline is working flawlessly using immutable Android system signatures.

We do this by completely ignoring the target game binary and targeting the invariant Linux Kernel Signature Node.

docs.title: 🧱 Layered Verification Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Before executing a single game plugin decryption routine, the orchestrator application can run this sequential checklist to pinpoint the exact failure layer:

Introspection Initialization Validation Pipeline
 │
 ├── [Checkpoint 1: Win32 Allocation Mapping] 
 │    └── Test: Locate MuMuNxDevice.exe process space and isolate 1.5625 GB / 3.4375 GB segments.
 │    └── Failure Meaning: Hypervisor base addresses shifted or ASLR rules altered. (Core SDK Error)
 │
 ├── [Checkpoint 2: Linux Kernel Signature Scan]
 │    └── Test: Sweep high memory for the invariant 'swapper\0' string and verify PID == 0.
 │    └── Failure Meaning: Android 15 kernel data layout or page table structure altered. (Core SDK Error)
 │
 └── [Checkpoint 3: Hardware MMU Table Walk Verification]
      └── Test: Read the init_task page structures manually using the 48-bit shift emulator.
      └── Failure Meaning: Page size scaling factor or table-entry masks are misaligned. (Core SDK Error)

docs.title: 🛡️ Boundary Control Isolation Rules
docs.text:
Isolating Core SDK Layer Faults from Game Obfuscation Faults

If Checkpoints 1, 2, and 3 Pass PerfectlyIf Checkpoint 2 or 3 Fails
  • Diagnostic Verdict: The hypervisor abstraction layer, your C# Win32 mapping engine, and your out-of-process ARM64 48-bit page table walker are 100% correct.
  • Action Plan: If the output data stream returns corrupt bytes after this point, you can completely ignore your core SDK infrastructure. The bug resides strictly within the game plugin's IL2CPP v31 metadata decryption algorithm, the HybridCLR interpreter parsing loop, or a localized pointer bit-shift routine.
  • Diagnostic Verdict: Your core infrastructure is blind or unaligned.
  • Action Plan: Do not touch your game plugin code. Lock down the game reversing files and focus entirely on auditing your MemoryMapper section sweep requirements or checking your MmuEmulator left-shift scaling mechanics against your third-party VMMap logs.

docs.text:
Hardware Isolation Rules

  • The Invariant Test Target: The Core SDK should feature a compilation configuration tag named #DEBUG_VMI_CORE. When toggled, the application attempts to read out the native Android kernel build version string directly from its invariant system space. If this string resolves cleanly, it proves your host scanner has a perfect, clear window straight into live target memory space.
  • Complete Decoupling from Brotli/HybridCLR: The hardware mapping engine must never import compression libraries or utilize runtime script parsing objects. It deals exclusively with flat, raw memory arrays.

docs.title: Logging & Diagnostic Infrastructure Specification
docs.text: This document maps the architectural requirements for the unified core logging extension engine running natively within the .NET 10 introspection solution framework.

docs.title: 🧭 Functional Logging Objectives
docs.text:
• Capture low-level hypervisor status updates, bit-shift milestones, and memory mapping exceptions cleanly across all projects.
  • Support a Runtime Dynamically Settable Log Filter Level via an on-the-fly dropdown selector (ranging from absolute blackout mode to high-frequency verbosity).
  • Provide an Independent Source-Muting Matrix allowing the user to uncheck and isolate specific code modules completely.
  • Decouple Text Formatting Entirely: Eliminate string interpolation at the call-site. Services emit raw data structures; formatting is handled downstream via a specialized extension module.
  • Capture detailed Call-Site Metadata automatically via compile-time injection attributes.

docs.title: 🧱 Non-Allocating Structured Payload Specification
docs.text:
To completely eliminate call-site string creation overhead, logging endpoints accept raw data message templates. The log event is transmitted as a thin primitive package:

public readonly record struct LogEventRecord(
    DateTime Timestamp,          // Precise clock capture time
    LogLevel Level,              // Severity flag
    string SourceComponent,      // Assembly module or Namespace identity
    string MessageTemplate,      // Invariant string format skeleton (e.g., "Walked PGD index {0} to GPA {1}")
    object[] PayloadArgs,        // Raw, un-rendered data parameters (ulong, int, etc.)
    string ExceptionDetails,     // Optional stacktrace data for Error/Fatal lines
    string CallingFile,          // Filename via [CallerFilePath]
    string CallingMethod,        // Method name via [CallerMemberName]
    int CallingLine              // Line number via [CallerLineNumber]
);

docs.text:
The text rendering block is extracted completely away from your real-time processing threads. String compilation runs downhill inside a Dedicated Formatting Extension only after filtering boundaries are cleared:

docs.text:
Absolute Formatting & Performance Invariants

  • The Invariant Call-Site Allocation Prohibition: Developers and AI engines are strictly forbidden from writing string interpolation blocks ($"GVA: {gva}") inside high-frequency processing methods. Messages must be passed as static templates, shifting string formatting tasks completely to the background.
  • Atomic Filter Short-Circuit: If a component fires an entry that is blocked by the active global dropdown level or an unchecked source checkbox, the runtime must drop the execution stack before any array boxing or object allocation occurs.
  • Isolated Formatter Responsibility: The text layout string formatting extension is completely self-contained. It takes the immutable LogEventRecord data, combines the message template with its primitive arguments, prepends the call-site source signatures ([MmuEmulator.cs:Line 42]), and pushes a single, finalized string line to your console or your Avalonia UI diagnostics monitor panel.

docs.title: Master Ticker Engine & Game Loop Synchronization
docs.text: This document establishes the specifications for the central, delta-time driven tick engine designed to synchronize logging, background memory tasks, and display rendering cycles.

docs.title: 🧭 The Low-Overhead Game-Loop Philosophy
docs.text:
To avoid asynchronous processing drift without choking host processor cycles, the entire SDK application maps its execution timeline to a unified, low-overhead Master Ticker Engine. Modeled after a game engine's core architecture, this service runs a continuous clock pass, computes the exact Delta Time (Δ t) since the last tick, and dispatches a synchronized execution intent down the central message bus.

    end

    subgraph Messaging [System Message Bus]

    end

        MB -->|Sync Interval: 50ms - 100ms| S1[Memory Mapper / MMU Worker Thread]

docs.title: 🧱 The Delta-Time Synchronization Frame Contract
docs.text:
Every processing cycle is bound tightly to an immutable tick message structure passed downhill to listening modules:

public readonly record struct EngineTickFrame(
    ulong FrameIndex,       // Monotonically increasing index tracking total loop passes
    double DeltaTime,       // Time elapsed since last tick (expressed in fractional seconds)
    double TotalRuntime     // Total elapsed execution runtime since engine boot
);

docs.title: ⚙️ Subsystem Synchronization Requirements
docs.text: When an EngineTickFrame intent drops down the system message bus, subscribing tasks must execute their step-by-step logic sequentially based on the relaxed interval rate:

docs.title: 1. Introspection Workers (MemoryMapper / MmuEmulator)
docs.text: • Action: The worker uses the delta interval to execute memory page translations. Because the target update loop is throttled to 50ms–100ms, the engine avoids choking the Windows thread scheduler, allowing brute-force page-walk lookups to execute cleanly without spiking CPU utilization.

docs.title: 2. Log Broker Flushes (LogBroker)
docs.text: • Action: Log packets generated across thread pools are held inside a thread-safe queue. Upon receiving the master frame tick, the LogBroker flushes the log queue in a single batch pass, grouping logs explicitly under the exact FrameIndex in which they occurred. Throttling this flush prevents constant, high-frequency disk I/O chatter.

docs.title: 3. Avalonia View Refreshes (MuMuSDK.Desktop)
docs.text: • Action: The user interface views listen for data-bound properties updated by the tick frame. Visual charts, log terminals, and readout overlays update their coordinate maps uniformly at the turn of the frame, completely eliminating visual stutter and out-of-sync data rendering.

docs.title: ⚠️ Master Ticker Safety & Performance Invariants
docs.text:
Absolute Master Loop Guardrails

  • Throttled Cycle Configuration: The master clock ticker must incorporate a configurable delay threshold set by default between 50ms and 100ms (10 to 20 Hz processing cadence). This keeps the engine highly responsive to live data changes while completely insulating the host PC from processor starvation.
  • High-Precision Clock Mandate: The tick calculator must leverage native hardware counters via System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp() to prevent clock drift issues caused by standard operating system thread scheduling.
  • Frame Stutter Insulation: If a specific game plugin or a heavy logging disk write takes too long and blows past the allocated frame budget, it must never block the master tick engine loop. The loop calculates the subsequent delta time dynamically, allowing the system to handle the lag spike safely without crashing the hypervisor memory tracking channels.

docs.title: Reactive Intent-Driven Presentation Architecture
docs.text: This document defines the structural requirements for an asynchronous, message-driven Avalonia UI platform utilizing an Intent/Publish-Subscribe communication loop.

docs.title: 🧭 The Fire-and-Forget Intent Pipeline
docs.text:
To achieve complete isolation, the presentation layer utilizes an Event-Driven Messaging Pattern. The user interface never invokes low-level core execution tasks directly; instead, it acts as an un-opinionated message terminal that broadcasts structural intents and updates its display grids exclusively based on inbound background telemetry packets.

  [ AVALONIA UI WINDOW ] ─── (Dispatches Fire-and-Forget) ───► [ SYSTEM MESSAGE BUS ]
           ▲                                                            │
           │ (Listens / Data-Binds Stream)                              ▼ (Triggers Worker)
  [ UI Thread State ]    ◄─── (Pushes Safe UI Strings) ───────── [ BACKGROUND WORKER ]

docs.title: 🧱 Intent and Event Message Contracts
docs.text: The communication loop between the presentation window and the backend background thread workers is governed by explicit message models defined inside MuMuSDK.Core.Interfaces:

docs.title: 1. The Intent Channel (Uphill to Downhill)
docs.text: Intents represent user actions dispatched from the UI view. They are immutable, fire-and-forget message payloads: * StartIntrospectionIntent(string packageCommName): Requests initialization of the hypervisor layout scan. * ExecutePointerCrawlIntent(ulong anchorGva, uint depth): Triggers the background brute-force crawler engine loop.

docs.title: 2. The Telemetry Stream (Downhill to Uphill)
docs.text: Workers process intents completely out-of-process on background threads, transforming memory cells into text primitives, and streaming them back up to the UI: * HypervisorStateEvent(bool isConnected, IntPtr lowerBaseHva, IntPtr upperBaseHva): Signals layout synchronization status. * GameMetricPayload(string metricName, string formattedValue): Delivers real-time de-obfuscated values (e.g., Health, Coordinates) formatted safely as string primitives ready for instant UI data-binding.

docs.title: 🛡️ Presentation Safety Invariants
docs.text:
Absolute Reactive UI Invariants

  • The Command Dispatch Isolation Rule: Avalonia click event handlers (ReactiveCommand) are strictly restricted to calling .Publish() or .Send() on the underlying system message bus. They are forbidden from awaiting a long-running memory translation task.
  • The Thread Context Dispatcher Mandate: Inbound data events streaming from background workers must pass explicitly through the Avalonia thread scheduler (Dispatcher.UIThread.Post) before touching UI-bound properties to prevent cross-thread rendering exceptions.

docs.title: 15-Scenario Core Integration Verification Matrix
docs.text: This document outlines the strict, sequential manual verification scenarios that must be executed and validated in order. No automated orchestration loops may be written until all 15 checkpoints pass cleanly with 100% predictable, documented data outputs.

docs.title: 🧭 The Progression Rule: No Skipping, No Guessing
docs.text:
Execution Mandate

If a test scenario returns an unaligned value, a null pointer, or an unexpected byte sequence, development halts immediately. You are completely forbidden from moving to the next tier or allowing an AI to propose a workaround. The underlying assumption must be corrected at the current failure site.

docs.title: 🧱 Phase 1: Host Process and Infrastructure Mapping
🟩 Scenario 1: Logging Extension Filtering and Short-Circuit Test
docs.text:
• Action: Set the global log filter dropdown to Info. Trigger a manual loop that fires 10,000 Trace entries.
  • Expected Output: Zero console output, zero disk writes, and zero memory heap allocation spike (verifying the atomic short-circuit protection is working with zero CPU overhead).

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 2: Downhill Log Formatter Extraction Test
docs.text:
• Action: Trigger a deliberate Info entry inside your memory mapper class with two primitive arguments (ulong, int).
  • Expected Output: The downstream log formatter extension catches the record, correctly appends compile-time file placement signatures ([MemoryMapper.cs:Line XX]), and outputs a beautifully unified, text-rendered string to console/UI.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 3: Win32 Process Handle Verification
docs.text:
• Action: Execute your P/Invoke process scan targeting the specific worker thread identifier: MuMuNxDevice.exe.
  • Expected Output: Returns a valid, non-null Windows process context handle with active memory query permissions.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 4: Lower System Space Allocation Sweep
docs.text:
• Action: Run a linear allocation boundary scan across the process allocations filtering for MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_READWRITE, and MEM_PRIVATE.
  • Expected Output: Pinpoints an unmanaged memory block matching exactly 1.5625 GB in size. Capture its base Host Virtual Address (lowerBaseHva).

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 5: Upper Application Space Allocation Sweep
docs.text:
• Action: Continue the linear boundary scan across the host workspace allocations with the same filtering flags.
  • Expected Output: Pinpoints an unmanaged memory block matching exactly 3.4375 GB in size. Capture its base Host Virtual Address (upperBaseHva).

docs.title: 🧱 Phase 2: Guest Kernel & Task Chain Navigation
🟩 Scenario 6: High-Memory Kernel Signature Match
docs.text:
• Action: Execute a flat linear byte array sweep across high guest virtual memory space (0xFFFF...) targeting the unique 8-byte compiled ASCII signature: s w a p p e r \0.
  • Expected Output: Locates the exact starting coordinate of the head kernel signature block inside your unmanaged host memory pool.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 7: init_task PID 0 Structural Validation
docs.text:
• Action: Read a signed 4-byte integer exactly 0x4C8 bytes forward from your discovered swapper node base address.
  • Expected Output: Value reads exactly 0 (verifying that your TaskDescriptor sequential struct layout perfectly aligns with the active Android 15 kernel memory geometry).

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 8: Circular Doubly-Linked List Step Test
docs.text:
• Action: Read the 8-byte next pointer located at offset 0x30 of the init_task node, pass it through the HypervisorRouter, and step to the adjacent node.
  • Expected Output: Successfully lands on the next active system task descriptor node without throwing an memory reading exception or dropping into an infinite loop.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 9: Target Package Process Discovery
docs.text:
• Action: Run your manual task traversal loop all the way through the circular chain, checking offset 0x6A0 on every task node for your specific game's string identifier (e.g., com.Target.Game).
  • Expected Output: Loop cleanly terminates and returns the valid Host Virtual Address pointer mapping the target game's unique task_struct node.

docs.title: 🧱 Phase 3: Hardware MMU Page Walking & Translation
🟩 Scenario 10: Memory Manager Descriptor Pointer Validation
docs.text:
• Action: Read the 8-byte reference pointer located at offset 0x480 (mm_map) of your isolated target game task node.
  • Expected Output: Returns a non-null, valid coordinate value (verifying the target process owns an active user-mode memory map context).

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 11: PGD Root Entry Extraction
docs.text:
• Action: Follow the memory manager map pointer down to offset 0x40 inside the host RAM layout to extract the process's Page Global Directory (PGD) root.
  • Expected Output: Returns a valid Guest Physical Address coordinate mapping the structural head of that application's hardware paging hierarchies.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 12: Precision 48-Bit Virtual Address Disassembly
docs.text:
• Action: Pass a known game pointer address into your AddressDisassembler utility routine.
  • Expected Output: Correctly cuts the 64-bit address into clean, 9-bit indexing slices and isolates the exact lower 12-bit page cell offset matching standard ARM64 architecture layout specs.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 13: Manual Multi-Tiered Page Table Walk (The Ultimate Core Proof)
docs.text:
• Action: Step manually through the 4-level table hierarchy (PGD -> PUD -> PMD -> PTE) by applying index offsets and clearing hardware flags with your page alignment mask (0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL).
  • Expected Output: Resolves the final table line to reveal the absolute Guest Physical Address (GPA) frame mapping for that variable.

docs.title: 🟩 Scenario 14: Hypervisor Route & MMIO Hole Verification
docs.text:
• Action: Hand your resolved GPA frame over to your HypervisorRouter service.
  • Expected Output: Properly identifies if the coordinate sits above or below the virtual MMIO hardware gap boundary and returns the absolute, translated Host Virtual Address (HVA) pointer.

docs.title: 🧱 Phase 4: Dynamic Presentation and Plugin Binding
🟩 Scenario 15: Asynchronous Intent-Driven Presentation Sync
docs.text:
• Action: Dispatch a StartIntrospectionIntent from your Avalonia UI view via your fire-and-forget message bus. Relax the master ticker engine to a steady 100ms delta-cadence.
  • Expected Output: The background worker picks up the intent, maps the process, loops the ticker, and pushes thread-safe string metrics back uphill across the bus channel—updating your desktop interface log stream and display elements uniformly without a single micro-stutter or cross-thread exception.

docs.title: Service Specification: Memory Mapping Engine
docs.text:
This module defines the structural requirements for scanning, filtering, and mapping the Windows host memory blocks assigned to the hypervisor runtime.

Functional Objectives

  • Dynamically bind to the active host worker process context (MuMuNxDevice.exe) 1.
  • Isolate the raw unmanaged memory segments representing the guest phone's physical hardware RAM.
  • Cache invariant Host Virtual Address (HVA) base anchors to eliminate redundant scanning overhead.

docs.title: 🧱 Algorithmic Scan Filtering Requirements
docs.text:
Host Memory Allocation Segment
 ├── State    == MEM_COMMIT      --> Filter out uncommitted virtual pages
 ├── Protect  == PAGE_READWRITE  --> Target mutable data execution streams
 └── Type     == MEM_PRIVATE     --> Target anonymous pagefile-backed components

Target Buffer Specifications

Memory Segment Block Target Physical Limit Expected Host Protection Mask Lower RAM Allocation 1.5625 GB PAGE_READWRITE Upper RAM Allocation 3.4375 GB PAGE_READWRITE

docs.title: ⚠️ Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Dynamic Discovery and Footprint Rules

  • No Hardcoded Base Offsets: Pointers must be fetched dynamically on initialization to survive host address space layout randomization (ASLR).
  • Cache Allocation Lifecycle: The base Host Virtual Addresses (HVA) remain completely static while an emulator session is alive. Cache these handles immediately at launch to bypass tracking validation overhead.

  1. Enforced via target system process scraping mechanisms. ↩

docs.title: Service Specification: Hardware MMU Emulator
docs.text:
This module defines the bitmask geometries and multi-tiered table traversal algorithms required to emulate an ARM64 Memory Management Unit (MMU) completely out-of-process.

Functional Objectives

  • Deconstruct standard 64-bit application virtual memory pointers into precise architectural coordinate slices.
  • Manually traverse the 4-level paging directory arrays inside the unmanaged host buffer stream.
  • Translate dynamic Guest Virtual Addresses (GVA) into invariant Guest Physical Addresses (GPA).

docs.title: 🧱 Mathematical Page Table Walking Rules
docs.text:
Under a standard 48-bit virtual address indexing map, an incoming pointer functions as an array of structured coordinate indices. The emulator cuts the pointer into 9-bit indexing slices to resolve physical destination cells:

  • Index Selection Mask (\(\text{Mask}_{\text{idx}}\)): 0x1FF
  • Page Offset Selection Mask (\(\text{Mask}_{\text{offset}}\)): 0xFFF
\[\text{Index} = (\text{GVA} \gg \text{Shift}) \ \& \ \text{0x1FF}\] 
64-Bit Guest Virtual Address (GVA) Pointer Input
 ├── Bits [47:39] ──► PGD Index (Page Global Directory Root Offset)
 ├── Bits [38:30] ──► PUD Index (Page Upper Directory Table Offset)
 ├── Bits [29:21] ──► PMD Index (Page Middle Directory Table Offset)
 ├── Bits [20:12] ──► PTE Index (Hardware Page Table Entry Base Offset)
 └── Bits [11:0]  ──► Page Offset (Absolute Byte Target Inside 4096-Byte Page Frame)

docs.title: ⚠️ Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Scale Precision and Alignment Verification

  • Descriptor Scale Factor: Every directory entry consumed within an ARM64 architecture table requires exactly 8 bytes of storage 1. The indices must be shifted left by 3 bits (\(\ll 3\)) before appending them to structural base locations.
  • Flag Bit Clearing: All raw pointers pulled from intermediate directory lines must clear flag markers by executing bitwise masking alongside the hardware frame boundary mask 0x0000FFFFFFFFF000UL before traversing down to subsequent directory tiers.

  1. Equivalent to standard 64-bit reference address elements. ↩

docs.title: Service Specification: Process Chain Enumerator
docs.text:
This module defines the requirements for navigating the guest operating system's internal scheduler structures out-of-process to find the target game's memory context.

Functional Objectives

  • Locate the unshifting system kernel anchor head node (init_task / PID 0).
  • Traverse the kernel's doubly-linked process array lists cleanly from the host layer.
  • Isolate the exact task node matching the target game application.

docs.text:

docs.title: ⚠️ Architectural Invariants & Alignment Constraints
docs.text:
64-Bit ARM Linux Geometry Bounds

The internal structure layouts and structural offsets are explicitly bound to the guest Android 15 kernel architecture. Modifying or overriding these metrics without corresponding documentation updates is strictly prohibited:

  • task_list Offset: 0x30
  • mm_map Pointer Offset: 0x480
  • process_id Offset: 0x4C8
  • process_comm Offset: 0x6A0
  1. 🔗 Links circular doubly-linked active execution structures.
  2. 🗺️ Memory manager reference hook used to extract translation registers.
  3. 🆔 Target validation identifier token.
  4. 🏷️ 16-character alphanumeric string descriptor tracking the task name.
